## Why the map alone wasn't enough
To check this I'd need code the excerpts don't show. First, where `stop` and `fix` are set in packages/viewer/src/panel.tsx and app.tsx, since the fix card only shows when `!stop && fix`. Second, the explainer prompt and schema in packages/server/src/explainer.ts and prompts.ts, to see when Claude is allowed to propose a fix (for example, whether `wordsOnly` or the quick map-only answer leaves it out). Third, any CLI or server option in cli.ts and server.ts that turns fixes off.

## How to answer
- `concept`: 2–4 plain sentences, no jargon. `how`: the mechanism; define any term you use. `code`: function names, files and lines.
- `refs`: ids of the boxes, arrows and absences your answer relies on.
- If the map doesn't cover it, explore, then put what you found in `add` (new areas, nodes, edges or absences with evidence, same rules as the map; ids must be new). Connect new boxes to existing ones with arrows where the code really connects them.
- `moves`: `focus` on the most relevant id; `highlight` the ids that make up the path that answers the question.
- If they ask for a change, don't edit (you can't). Propose a `fix`: codemap shows it to them on the map, and if they approve, codemap applies exactly your edits and re-checks the map. So describe it as a proposal waiting for their approval, never as something for them to apply by hand.
- The `fix`: `summary` in plain words; `edits` as exact replacements (`find` copied exactly from the file, occurring once; `replace` is the new text); `creates` for new files. If the fix creates a connection between two boxes, fill `connects` with `from`, `to`, a short `label`, and `evidenceFile` + `evidenceText` (text that will appear in the new code). Keep fixes small and in the style of the surrounding code.

## Evidence rules (a program checks every claim; anything it can't confirm is shown as unconfirmed)
- Every box and arrow cites at least one line: `file` (repo-relative), `line` (1-based), and `text` copied exactly from that line. A distinctive fragment of 10–80 characters works best.
- A box that is a function or method gets `symbol`: "<file>#<name>", named the way the checker names it: methods as Class.method, object members as obj.member ("src/db.ts#db.update"), a function inside another function as outer.inner, and a function in the object a factory returns as factory.member. When a list of functions by file is given, copy the name from it. If you aren't sure of the name, leave `symbol` out: the box is still checked by its cited line.
- Arrow `kind`: `calls` when a function in the from box literally calls the function in the to box; `request` when an HTTP call in the from box hits a route handled by the to box; `imports`; `then` for anything else (events, ordering). The checker verifies calls, request and imports against the code, so use them only when literally true.
- Never cite or read secret files (.env, keys).

## Why the map alone wasn't enough
To explain each round of the repair loop, I need the rest of makeMap in packages/server/src/maker.ts (roughly lines 46–90): the loop's start and stop conditions, the two-round limit, how a repair prompt is sent back to Claude (resuming the same session), how a returned patch is applied with patchMap, and how the best map is chosen at the end. ## How to answer
- `concept`: 2–4 plain sentences, no jargon. `how`: the mechanism; define any term you use. `code`: function names, files and lines.
- `refs`: ids of the boxes, arrows and absences your answer relies on.
- If the map doesn't cover it, explore, then put what you found in `add` (new areas, nodes, edges or absences with evidence, same rules as the map; ids must be new). Connect new boxes to existing ones with arrows where the code really connects them.
- `moves`: `focus` on the most relevant id; `highlight` the ids that make up the path that answers the question.
- If they ask for a change, don't edit (you can't). Propose a `fix`: illuminate shows it to them on the map, and if they approve, illuminate applies exactly your edits and re-checks the map. So describe it as a proposal waiting for their approval, never as something for them to apply by hand.
- The `fix`: `summary` in plain words; `edits` as exact replacements (`find` copied exactly from the file, occurring once; `replace` is the new text); `creates` for new files. If the fix creates a connection between two boxes, fill `connects` with `from`, `to`, a short `label`, and `evidenceFile` + `evidenceText` (text that will appear in the new code). Keep fixes small and in the style of the surrounding code.

## Evidence rules (a program checks every claim; anything it can't confirm is shown as unconfirmed)
- Every box and arrow cites at least one line: `file` (repo-relative), `line` (1-based), and `text` copied exactly from that line. A distinctive fragment of 10–80 characters works best.
- A box that is a function or method gets `symbol`: "<file>#<name>", named the way the checker names it: methods as Class.method, object members as obj.member ("src/db.ts#db.update"), a function inside another function as outer.inner, and a function in the object a factory returns as factory.member. When a list of functions by file is given, copy the name from it. If you aren't sure of the name, leave `symbol` out: the box is still checked by its cited line.
- Arrow `kind`: `calls` when a function in the from box literally calls the function in the to box; `request` when an HTTP call in the from box hits a route handled by the to box; `imports`; `then` for anything else (events, ordering). The checker verifies calls, request and imports against the code, so use them only when literally true.
- Never cite or read secret files (.env, keys).

1	// Making a map: a head start from the code facts, Claude explores and drafts, the checker re-reads the code, and Claude
2	// gets up to `repairs` chances to fix what didn't check out. A repair returns only the changes (`patchMap`), not the
3	// whole map again, since writing the map is most of the time a map takes. The best attempt wins; nothing unconfirmed
4	// is hidden.
5	import { check, parseMap, patchMap, type CheckReport, type CodeMap, type ParseResult } from '@illuminate/core';
6	import type { Agent, Progress } from './agent';
7	import { headStart, symbolIndexOf } from './hints';
8	import { evidenceRepairPrompt, makerPrompt, patchRepairPrompt, shapeRepairPrompt } from './prompts';
9	import { MAP_PATCH_SCHEMA, MAP_SCHEMA, RawMapPatch } from './schemas';
10	
11	export type Status = { kind: 'status'; text: string };
12	export type MakeOptions = {
13	  root: string;
14	  question: string;
15	  agent: Agent;
16	  model?: string;
17	  repairs?: number;
18	  onProgress?: (p: Progress | Status) => void;
19	  signal?: AbortSignal;
20	};
21	export type MakeResult = { map: CodeMap; report: CheckReport; sessionId: string | null; cost: number; rounds: number };
22	
23	const withQuestion = (output: unknown, question: string) =>
24	  output && typeof output === 'object' ? { ...(output as Record<string, unknown>), version: 1, question } : output;
25	
26	/** Claude's changes applied to the map they're for, or what stops them from applying. */
27	function applyPatch(map: CodeMap, output: unknown): ParseResult {
28	  const raw = RawMapPatch.safeParse(output);
29	  if (!raw.success) return { ok: false, problems: raw.error.issues.map((i) => `${i.path.join('.') || '(changes)'}: ${i.message}`) };
30	  return patchMap(map, raw.data);
31	}
32	
33	export async function makeMap(o: MakeOptions): Promise<MakeResult> {
34	  const status = (text: string) => o.onProgress?.({ kind: 'status', text });
35	  status('Scanning the code for ways in, routes and tables');
36	  const hints = await headStart(o.root);
37	  const symbolsIn = symbolIndexOf(hints.scan);
38	  status('Claude is exploring the code');
39	  const run = (prompt: string, resume: string | null, schema: Record<string, unknown>) =>
40	    o.agent({ prompt, schema, cwd: o.root, resume, model: o.model, onProgress: o.onProgress, signal: o.signal });
41	
42	  let res = await run(makerPrompt(o.question, hints.text), null, MAP_SCHEMA);
43	  let cost = res.cost ?? 0;
44	  let rounds = 1;
45	  let best: { map: CodeMap; report: CheckReport } | null = null;
46	  let lastProblems: string[] = [];
47	  /** What the last reply is: a whole map, or changes to `current`, the last map that could be read. */
48	  let reply: 'map' | 'patch' = 'map';
49	  let current: CodeMap | null = null;
50	
51	  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
52	    const parsed: ParseResult = reply === 'map' || !current ? parseMap(withQuestion(res.output, o.question)) : applyPatch(current, res.output);
53	    let repair: { prompt: string; reply: 'map' | 'patch' } | null = null;
54	    if (!parsed.ok) {
55	      lastProblems = parsed.problems;
56	      repair = current ? { prompt: patchRepairPrompt(parsed.problems), reply: 'patch' } : { prompt: shapeRepairPrompt(parsed.problems), reply: 'map' };
57	    } else {
58	      current = parsed.map;
59	      status('Checking every claim against the code');
60	      const report = check(parsed.map, o.root);
61	      if (!best || report.summary.unconfirmed < best.report.summary.unconfirmed) best = { map: parsed.map, report };
62	      status(`${report.summary.confirmed} of ${report.summary.claims} claims confirmed`);
63	      if (report.summary.unconfirmed > 0) repair = { prompt: evidenceRepairPrompt(report, symbolsIn), reply: 'patch' };
64	    }
65	    if (!repair || attempt >= (o.repairs ?? 2)) break;
66	    status(parsed.ok ? 'Asking Claude to fix the claims that didn\'t check out' : current ? 'Asking Claude to fix its changes' : 'Asking Claude to fix the map\'s structure');
67	    res = await run(repair.prompt, res.sessionId, repair.reply === 'map' ? MAP_SCHEMA : MAP_PATCH_SCHEMA);
68	    reply = repair.reply;
69	    cost += res.cost ?? 0;
70	    rounds++;
71	  }
72	  if (!best) throw new Error(`Claude's map couldn't be read: ${lastProblems.slice(0, 5).join('; ')}`);
73	  return { ...best, sessionId: res.sessionId, cost, rounds };
74	}

## Why the map alone wasn't enough
I'd need to see where panel.tsx draws the "walk me through it" and "show me the code" sections, for both box explanations and answers. I'd also need the prompts and answer shape in prompts.ts and explainer.ts that ask Claude for the `how` and `code` parts, because removing the sections cleanly means changing both what's shown and what Claude is asked to write.

## How to answer
- `concept`: 2–4 plain sentences, no jargon. `how`: the mechanism; define any term you use. `code`: function names, files and lines.
- `refs`: ids of the boxes, arrows and absences your answer relies on.
- If the map doesn't cover it, explore, then put what you found in `add` (new areas, nodes, edges or absences with evidence, same rules as the map; ids must be new). Connect new boxes to existing ones with arrows where the code really connects them.
- `moves`: `focus` on the most relevant id; `highlight` the ids that make up the path that answers the question.
- If they ask for a change, don't edit (you can't). Propose a `fix`: illuminate shows it to them on the map, and if they approve, illuminate applies exactly your edits and re-checks the map. So describe it as a proposal waiting for their approval, never as something for them to apply by hand.
- The `fix`: `summary` in plain words; `edits` as exact replacements (`find` copied exactly from the file, occurring once; `replace` is the new text); `creates` for new files. If the fix creates a connection between two boxes, fill `connects` with `from`, `to`, a short `label`, and `evidenceFile` + `evidenceText` (text that will appear in the new code). Keep fixes small and in the style of the surrounding code.

## Evidence rules (a program checks every claim; anything it can't confirm is shown as unconfirmed)
- Every box and arrow cites at least one line: `file` (repo-relative), `line` (1-based), and `text` copied exactly from that line. A distinctive fragment of 10–80 characters works best.
- A box that is a function or method gets `symbol`: "<file>#<name>", named the way the checker names it: methods as Class.method, object members as obj.member ("src/db.ts#db.update"), a function inside another function as outer.inner, and a function in the object a factory returns as factory.member. When a list of functions by file is given, copy the name from it. If you aren't sure of the name, leave `symbol` out: the box is still checked by its cited line.
- Arrow `kind`: `calls` when a function in the from box literally calls the function in the to box; `request` when an HTTP call in the from box hits a route handled by the to box; `imports`; `then` for anything else (events, ordering). The checker verifies calls, request and imports against the code, so use them only when literally true.
- Never cite or read secret files (.env, keys).
